svg.aria-label: The real three-way handshake between the Pi and example.org's server, with sequence numbers and options

g.text: 30.2 ms after the SYN: one round trip
established: from now on, count from 0

ol.li: The Pi sends a segment with the SYN flag (“synchronize”) and no data. Its sequence number is its initial sequence number, picked at random. The options say what it can do: take segments of up to 1,460 bytes, understand selective acknowledgements and timestamps, and multiply its window by 210.

The server answers with SYN and ACK together. It acknowledges the Pi’s SYN by expecting byte 1912436192 next (a SYN counts as one byte, even though it carries none), and picks its own random starting number, and its own options.
The Pi acknowledges the server’s SYN. Three segments, one and a half round trips, and both sides know the other’s starting number. The Pi can send data straight after this ACK, and does, 3 ms later.
Because the real numbers are huge and random, tools like tcpdump, Wireshark and this chapter’s lab usually show them relative to the starting number: the first byte of data is byte 1.

figure.figcaption: The three-way handshake, from the real capture (Chapter 13 invented it; here are the numbers).
